# Description of Greece, volume 1

## Identity and consulted witness

Pausanias, Description of Greece, trans. W. H. S. Jones, vol. 1 (Harvard/Heinemann, 1918), Fordham transcription. [Selected digital carrier](https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/ancient/pausanias-bk1.asp). Accessed and saved 8 September 2026. The raw response is retained at `working/sources-texts-references/primary-texts/attica/pausanias-description-greece-jones-1918.html` (SHA-256 `72810a6b8b06e8eabdb1390c623067118ad4b102314e22e4add2c9d6f9c397fc`). A saved page can contain more material than the selected reading; no whole-work reading is claimed.

## Source-specific reading

The description moves through a sacred precinct: Zeus’s altar outside the entrance; inside, Poseidon with Erechtheus, Butes and Hephaestus; family paintings; a double building, sea-water cistern and trident mark. The reported sound under a south wind and the legend of Poseidon’s evidence belong to the account without becoming independent archaeological observations. Athena’s city-wide honour leads to her image and the lamp attributed to Callimachus. Its yearly oil supply is described separately from the contest olive.

The subsequent olive paragraph names Athena’s testimony, reports regrowth to two cubits on the day of burning, and locates Pandrosus’s adjoining sanctuary. The report differs from Herodotus’s next-day shoot of about one cubit. Preserving both accounts gives the place its literary plurality; merging the timings would remove evidence rather than reconcile it.
